The most underrated BEST jrpg I've played in forever, or ever

Echoes of Aetheria, developed and published by Dancing Dragon Games, is a deliberate throwback to the era of classic turn-based Japanese RPGs, built with a clear affection for the structure and sensibilities of 16-bit adventures. It embraces a familiar formula—party-based combat, world-spanning conflict, and a steadily unfolding narrative—but attempts to refine that foundation with modern pacing and a stronger emphasis on character interaction. The result is a game that feels immediately recognizable to genre veterans, yet polished enough to remain accessible to newer players.

The story opens with a relatively personal incident that quickly spirals into a broader tale of political tension, war, and shifting alliances between nations. While the overarching narrative leans on familiar tropes, it gains momentum through its cast of characters, each bringing distinct personalities and motivations into the journey. Dialogue plays a significant role in keeping the experience engaging, often injecting humor or emotional weight into otherwise conventional plot developments. Even when the story follows predictable beats, the interactions between party members help maintain a sense of investment, giving the narrative a more human core than its premise might initially suggest.

Combat is structured around a traditional turn-based system, but it introduces small refinements that add a layer of tactical consideration. Abilities operate on cooldowns, and resource management becomes an important factor in determining how aggressively players can approach encounters. This encourages a more thoughtful rhythm in battles, where timing and planning matter more than simply selecting the strongest attack. Early and mid-game encounters benefit from this design, offering a satisfying balance between challenge and accessibility. However, as the game progresses, patterns begin to emerge, and optimal strategies can reduce the need for experimentation, making later battles feel less dynamic than they initially do.

Exploration is a central component of the experience, with dungeons and environments designed to encourage navigation and discovery rather than passive traversal. Puzzles involving switches, pathways, and hidden elements add variety to the journey, while the absence of random encounters helps maintain a smoother pace. This design choice allows players to engage with the world on their own terms, avoiding the frustration of constant interruptions. That said, some areas can feel overly extended, and the limited variety in enemies and environmental design may cause certain sections to feel repetitive, particularly during longer play sessions.

One of the more engaging systems is the crafting mechanic, which provides a degree of customization in character progression. By collecting materials and forging equipment, players can tailor their party’s strengths and experiment with different builds. While not overly complex, this system adds a meaningful layer of strategy that complements the combat mechanics. It breaks up the standard progression loop and gives players a sense of control over how their party evolves, even if the overall impact remains relatively modest.

Visually, the game adheres to a retro-inspired aesthetic that prioritizes clarity over innovation. Character sprites and environments are functional and cohesive, though they rarely stand out in a crowded field of RPG Maker titles. The presentation succeeds in evoking nostalgia, but it does little to distinguish itself beyond that familiarity. The soundtrack, on the other hand, contributes more effectively to the experience, offering a range of compositions that enhance both exploration and combat while reinforcing the game’s tone.

Where Echoes of Aetheria shows its limitations is in its consistency. The pacing of the narrative can feel uneven, with certain developments occurring too quickly to fully resonate. Similarly, while the gameplay systems are solid, they do not evolve significantly over time, leading to a sense that the experience plateaus rather than building toward a more complex or rewarding endgame. These issues do not overshadow the game’s strengths, but they do prevent it from reaching the level of depth and refinement seen in standout entries within the genre.

Ultimately, Echoes of Aetheria is a well-executed homage to classic RPG design, offering a comfortable and engaging experience that prioritizes familiarity and character-driven storytelling. It may not push the boundaries of the genre, but it delivers a steady and enjoyable adventure for those who appreciate its influences. Its charm lies in its sincerity and focus, even if its ambitions occasionally exceed its execution.

echoes of aetheria is a rpg developed by dancing dragon games that released in january 2016 for PC. it's their fourth game released on steam, and their most recent until they released their fifth game in 2022. it's a pretty standard affair if you're a fan of old-school RPGs, but the storyline is interesting enough to keep players engaged despite some cliches that will make you roll your eyes. the combat can get repetitive mostly due to the sheer amount of combat encounters you'll find. the art style is bright and colorful, especially when compared to other rpg-maker games. there's still no voice work which is disappointing but the music has a distinct charm and energy to it that makes it fit right in among games with good/great soundtracks. 

this is a fun game, definitely not the worst game dancing dragons has made, but i think there was a little too much fluff that makes the experience feel bloated. there are a lot of things that didn't need to be so cookie cutter when it comes to game design or rpg mechanics. there are definitely things to like, like no random encounters, no grinding, strategic combat, and even fun little quirky items that are surprisingly fun to come across. the biggest bright spot that i want to highlight is definitely the characters and how they're written. the devs have shown over their first four games that they have a knack for writing fun and interesting characters that always seem to fit right in to the setting the game they're in takes place. 

i have been extremely excited to eventually play symphony of war, their fifth and most recent release on steam, and now i have played all four of their earlier titles i feel confident to go in with an open mind and not be too overhyped. i think they really improved upon their past games so i'm hoping i'll still be pleasantly surprised when i play that for the first time.

as long as you're not expecting some masterpiece rpg, and you realize there are some things here that are simply just less polished, then i definitely recommend grabbing this on sale for extremely cheap and playing this if you have nothing else to play and are looking for a fresh rpg to try. most people will take anywhere from 20-30 hours to complete the main story but going for more of a completionist run like i do will put you closer to 40-50 hours instead, making this easily the biggest of the first four games released by the developer.

Echoes of Aetheria é um jogo indie feito no RPG Maler VX Ace.

O jogo utiliza um sistema de batalha original onde a formação do grupo influencia em diversas coisas, como: alcance das magias, chance de esquiva, dano recebido e chance de ser alvo de ataques inimigos. Alguns inimigos possuem uma habilidade que bagunça a sua formação, só que isso não é desfeito quando a batalha acaba, te obrigando a ir no menu de formação e reposicionar os personagens manualmente sempre que isso acontecer, o que incomoda um pouco.

Assim como nos demais jogos da Dancing Dragon Games, o jogo tem um notável salto de dificuldade nos últimos três chefes pra incentivar as sidequests, mas aqui é um pouco mais complicado já que você precisa tanto completar as batalhas de arena individuais para conseguir a receita das "Ultimate Weapons", quanto farmar metais raros como "Adamantite" e "Aetherium" (que só podem ser encontrados numa dungeon opcional no fim do jogo) para montar as armas e ter uma chance contra os chefes finais. 

O jogo é mais linear que a maioria e o mapa-mundi é no estilo "point-and-click". Ainda sim, é possível abortar a missão atual através do menu se precisar grindar. No geral, as dungeon tem tamanhos ideais, não sendo nem muito longas nem muito curtas; a unica parte que incomoda é um certo labirinto com efeito de loop. As dungeons também possuem puzzles, sempre no esquema de "procurar alavancas coloridas para abrir passagem" também presente na duologia "Deadly Sin" e em "Skyborn". A história é boa, mas também nota-se uma similaridade nela com a narrativa dos anteriores, em especial com a do "Deadly Sin 2".

Apesar dos problemas menores, Echoes of Aetheria é um jogo de RPG Maker muito bem feito. Recomendo.

I was inspired to check this game out after playing Dancing Dragon's most recent title, "Symphony of War". 
 While it's not anywhere nearly as good as SOW, it's still a pretty solid RPG that is well worth the price. It's basically just like SOW except you command a traditional 5-man RPG party instead of an army. The combat is good, the story is servicable, and I especially was impressed with how complex the dungeons were. In contrast to a game like say, Octopath Traveler, where all the dungeons are just straight paths with a corner or two for treasure, this one actually has big sprawling massive caverns that really make you work to find all the best loot. Even better, the enemy encounters are limited, so you don't have to fight random enemies every few seconds trying to find where to go.

The game also has a pretty good crafting system, though the menu information is frustratingly limited. The game doesn't show you if what you are creating is superior to what you already have, so you can sometimes have to do a lot of saving and reloading, which is thankfully quick.

The dialogue is amusingly modern for its setting, it actually gave me a laugh or two. There was this one character who kept calling one of my party members "prom queen", which led me to wonder if this medieval fantasy kingdom actually has proms. What a shame we never got to see those.

However, I do have to say the game's big weakness is that absurd technology mix-up. It isn't just a medieval fantasy with some steam-punk elements like SOW. EOA's universe has essentially Star Wars level technology, so it really doesn't make sense to have the population living in medieval cities or fighting with swords and bows. This aspect made it really hard to take the game or the plot seriously.

Plus the last boss has an insane difficulty spike. I cleared nearly the whole game on hard up to then, only to run into a final boss that one-shots all my party members with every hit. This still happened even on normal, so I just gave up and played on easy to be able to see the ending.

Overall though I'd say this is a good enjoyable game though. Certainly worth checking out if you are looking for something else to hold you over till SOW gets a sequel or update. And a good way to show your support for the company that gave us the excellent SOW to begin with.

Alright, now that I've played around with Echoes of Aetheria for a little while, I think I can safely say I can give my impressions on it.

Simply put...it's not what I was expecting, and that's not exactly a good thing in this case.

While I do like the slight tactical feel to the battle system, when a basic enemy that's like 10 levels below you is two-shotting people 10 levels above it, something is wrong. When you literally cannot equip any armor on any of your characters because it's too heavy for them, and yet the highest equipment you can give them at the time is nowhere near enough to beat enemies at their own level, something is wrong. When all your attacks with the strongest weapons in the game at that level are doing peanuts damage against even weaker enemies, something is wrong.

Why are none of my abilities doing what they should be doing? Why are none of the upgrades I give to said abilities actually doing anything? Why are 90% of the skills all five of the characters have essentially useless? Why does my healer literally have to kill herself halfway in order to heal one person? Hell, why do so many of her special attacks DAMAGE HER? Why is my level 33 character (who the game handed to me on a silver platter, I might add, while everyone else was at level 15), who has the most health, defense, strength, and magical power in the game so far, dying to level 15 opponents on normal difficulty?

I can't even see the enemies' stats in-game, I can't see what any of my own status effects do, and the turn system sometimes just has a mind of its own and switches around who goes first. This is NOT how you do an RPG battle system. You should AT LEAST be able to see the enemies' health bars somehow, either through targeting them or just normally.

And that's just the battle system, the story isn't getting much better to compensate. The characters are so flat it's actually incredible, and the dialogue is cringe-inducing. The plot is too fast-paced in the beginning and barely gives any time for the characters to breathe, and when it eventually does, it leaves the player unsatisfied with how little character growth is happening. And that's pretty much all I can say about it, because there really isn't that much else TO say. I've seen stories like it before, and yet those other ones at least tried to make it fun and adventurous. This one...doesn't. It's just there.

Finally, there's the rest of the gameplay: forging, exploring, and missions. Simply put, the dungeons barely have any real exploration in them (just searching for buttons to unlock some doors, and a key to unlock a chest...how riveting), and the treasures you do find are almost never worth it. The missions are bare-bones and extremely linear, there's no side-quests, there's no looking around, there's no world-building, there's not even any real exploration, you're just sent from one mission to the next without any overworld stuff. That's...lame.

And then the forging...where do I even begin? It's unintuitive, for starters. There's no guide, there's no tutorials, the game just throws it at you and says "go wild". Okay, but can I at least know the basics? Nope, not even that; okay. So I start forging, but the game doesn't even tell you what you're going to get when you forge something (all it gives is "???" on every stat for the equipment you're making), so you have no idea if you're going to waste some of your materials when you make it.

Sooooo yeah, not satisfied with this game at all. I was having fun at first, but the longer I played, the worse these problems got. I'm no longer having fun, and the moment that happens in a game is the moment I drop it.

遊戲最亮眼處是角色技能，每位角色有二十多種技能可以自由升級、配置，再加上十多種可選擇的被動技，與主動技相互搭配，讓每位角色都有很多元的戰術可塑性。且最佛心的是它的技能點可以隨時重新配置，若一套戰術用不順手，甚至只是心血來潮想換打法，隨時可以重新配置技能，不用任何代價。拜豐富的技能戰術所賜，這遊戲至少在前中期的戰鬥十分有趣。

裝備系統也有其特色。雖然初期較枯燥，但隨著遊戲進展，素材種類變得多元，會發現裝備鍛造有許多可挖掘的變化，與鑲嵌系統配合，也讓整備更添樂趣。然而鍛造的成果無法預覽，時常導致做出的裝備不如預期，只好倒回去讀取檔案重做，或是認賠浪費素材，是對使用者較不貼心的設計。

整個遊戲最難受的部分則是迷宮——這位作者前幾款作品的迷宮都挺有趣，充滿冒險感的迷宮規模與恰到好處的機關謎題，走起來十分舒適——但到了這一款，作者好像暴走了一樣(或許太執著超越自己的前作)，各種刻意叫玩家繞路的機關、邏輯複雜的岔路、巨大到讓人放棄記憶的地圖規模。再加上小怪群常常一次7~10隻撲上來，迷宮都走很累了，加上打怪更疲乏。但我還是乖乖把每一隻小怪都清掉了，因為迷宮大到難認，清掉小怪姑且可以當個路標……

通常玩RPG走迷宮都會努力把每一條路都搜遍，因為不想錯過寶箱。這款還是第一次就算明顯看到有沒開的寶箱我也不想去找的，因為累了。前面提到戰鬥多元性的樂趣，遊戲後期在疲乏的迷宮中也逐漸麻木了。

總結來說，如果玩家有興趣嘗試這個團隊的RPG作品，比起這款我更推薦上上款作品Deadly Sin 2，這款的優點Deadly Sin 2也都具備，只是稍樸素單純一些。不過Deadly Sin 2是傳統地雷式遇怪，可能有人比較不喜歡。小品向的Skyborn也是個選擇，雖然較無法見識這位作者的全力。至於這款EoA，以同團隊的作品而言我只會擺在第三順位吧，請抱持面對刁難的覺悟再嘗試(?)

最後附帶一提：這位作者的文學底子可能很不錯，英文用字比較深奧，也常常穿插俗諺俚語，閱讀起來比一般英文遊戲更困難些。不過劇情偏向王道，就算幾句話沒看懂也還是知道發生了什麼，因此就算英文苦手，可能也不用太擔心。

A fantastic modern take on a classic JRPG turn-based game! I highly recommend it for Final Fantasy lovers and anyone who is into the classic RPG game style. 

Firstly, I love the tall sprites and beautiful tile sets used for this game. This game really utilized RPG maker well but also, it's been made so professionally that you wouldn't even think it's really an RPG Maker game. Firstly, the story is great but what's even better are the awesome and well-developed characters, they are all very likeable. The story can get a little confusing along the way but I guess that's just me wanting to get through this game as this game is VERY long. At least for me it was.

The battle system is incredible, I love the grid-based system it uses to allow you to position your characters strategically for battle. I also love the skill points system for the characters and while for the most part, I found the battles and even bosses pretty easy, it gets EXTREMELY hard by the end of the game so just make sure you grind your characters up until level 75-80 on normal mode if you wish to defeat the final boss because I tried so many times before level 70 but I had to grind my characters up to level 80 just to defeat them (by then the final boss was actually pretty easy). It was a huge struggle and frustration that I had to make lots of time for grinding though. 

Other cons include that some of the puzzles in this game are a bit too hard and you often will find yourself getting lost. I wish there was an option from at least one of the characters to flee a battle in case you come across a monster in your path. By the end of the game, there was an exceptionally hard puzzle that took me a few days to figure out. It was really frustrating but overall, I do like puzzles but just make them a little easier and not like a maze. 

I like the crafting system in this. Overall, it was done well but the problem with it was that it doesn't tell you whether what you crafted will benefit any of the characters so I often got frustrated after finding out that certain equipment that was crafted was NOT increasing any of the character's stats that it's intended for meaning that I just wasted materials to craft that item...so it can be a bit frustrating too with the crafting system as it's like a guessing game even though I do like that it's a feature especially if done right. 

Sadly, I had to grind like CRAZY towards the end just to defeat the final boss so just be aware of that, a lot of preparation and time is needed for the ending part of the game... Apart from that, this has been a very enjoyable gameplay and I really liked the ending too. Amazing characters, battle system and soundtrack!

I really enjoyed Skyborn, but this game feels like it has a bit of a second system effect.

To explain:

In software dev a person may build their first system.  Because they're unsure with themselves, they'll be conservative.  Not building anything too fancy, too large, or too complex.  It will be successful.

When they build their second, they'll have more confidence and will be less conservative.  The result will be a system with tons of problems if it works at all.  This is an effect that's been recognized in the software industry for the last 30-40 years.

This game feels that way to me.

I'm sure the story is swell, but the fact that I would have to flip back and forth between my inventory and the shop (or crafting window) JUST to compare them is wholly and completely asinine.  Not to mention the byzantine levels that feel like the developer is pitting themselves against you.  Or making the player complete levels twice in order to get everything because the layout will physically change after the first run through.

These are all seem like fine ideas on paper, but miss the point of games, which is to be enjoyable and fun.

Echoes of Aetheria is one of the better JRPG-inspired RPGMaker games out there right now, and I think the best that Dancing Dragon has to offer, though most of their other games are also quite fun. 

The lore and environment is leaps and bounds larger than any other RPGMaker game that I have played, and I have played a fair few of them on offer here on Steam. That said, it's not so massive that it overextends its reach or scope, which is aided by a central plot line. Overall the plot has it's share of predictable and cliched moments, but has a few shocking moments and twists, again not commonly seen out of the RPGMaker scene. 

The music is especially a welcome surprised. I have listened to and played a fair share of multi-million dollar RPG projects with much inferior soundtracks to this game, and I don't think I could pay it a higher compliment than that. Anyone out there looking to hire talent, give Phil Hamilton a job. Though I guess that would be quite a blow to Dancing Dragon Games so... at least something to think about. 

The battle and crafting system is a huge step up from Skyborn and other similar games, as well. The grid based battle system offers a small level of strategy that is not often found in turn-based RPGs regardless of scale, and I greatly appreciate it. That said, I do feel like you quickly become overburdened with new skills at a rapid rate due to how fast you level. You'll end up learning 95% of all of your skills before you are halfway through the game, and then finally by the end of the game you will hopefully have a good grasp of what works and doesn't with your play style, but some better pacing would have went a long way to making that better. The crafting system, while not really any more complex than in Skyborn, does offer more variety. It's also not always so clear cut what is the "best" of any equipment either because not always does the "newest" and "shiniest" equipment make the best equipment. You are encouraged to play around a little, albeit very little, but still very much appreciated.

All that said, the game isn't without it's faults either. While not as grevious as other similar styled games, the use of labyrinthian design in RPGMaker games really needs to stop. I have chastised games for it in the past, and I will do so here, too. Labyrinths are nothing more than useless padding to inflate game time, no one likes them, and they only serve to possibly detract people away from the experience. Granted most of the mazes aren't overly complex in this game and you are usually rewarded with treasure for your troubles, but it can become a burden to navigate to a certain destination when you can't remember how to get from Point A to Point B. 

All in all, Echoes of Aetheria ranks very highly on my list as one of the best RPGMaker RPG games available to date. That's not say it doesn't have it's faults which continue to plague this sub-genre of RPGs, but said faults are far less glaring here than in most of it's contemporaries. Game is definitely worth picking up if you are at all interested in playing RPGMaker games, and even if you are a person who is on the fence about trying one, this is a great game to break into.

Been on the lookout for an old school SNES or Genesis style RPG lately (there's only so many times you can replay Chrono Trigger, Breath Of Fire, etc.) and went with this one after looking through a whoooooooooole lot of options. It hits all the right notes, and has a strong FF6 vibe with the combination of magic and tech. 

Adding a grid to the traditional turn based combat allows for some strategy, and each character has multiple skills to choose from and swap out depending on the enemies in the current area. Fire blades aren't much help against desert creatures for instance, while Soha's ability to influence humans is incredibly helpful when storming a castle and fighting an army. 

As to be expected from this sort of game, there are a few silly and cheesy lines in the dialog, but there's a darker edge to some of the character interactions and story beats. This is one of the few indie RPG Maker style games where all the plotting factions and groups with varying goals seem to gel together into a cohesive world that makes sense and draws you in to learn more as you go. 

Between the robust crafting system missing from most original SNES RPGs and the ability to choose difficulty options in each dungeon, Echoes of Aetheria does a lot right and not much wrong.

This is an enjoyable JRPG. If it was released 20-25 years ago during the 16/32 bit era, it would have been a highly successful RPG.   

Pros: 
The best part about this game is the combat which is downright fun and interesting.  I love how you can switch out abilities without penalty to try something new and how formation of your party actually matters.  Each character is loaded with different skills and you have access to almost all of them halfway through the game.  Also, if you do get smoked by an enemy, you can replay the battle without losing your progress which is a great touch.  

I really enjoyed the gameplay and puzzles that you experience at every level.  Although, some of them don't really make practical sense, I mean why is there a bunch of switches and buttons in a cave, but I thought they were a nice addition and fun to work through.  There is tons of loot so exploration was also a blast.  I would have enjoyed a world screen, it is absent here, but there is great detail in the environments and you can replay some levels.      

One of the best aspects of Echoes is the characters.  They are written really well and unlike most games where you only care for maybe one or two characters, I found myself caring for my entire party.  Each character is vastly different and we are given the proper time to explore their backstory and development.  

Cons:
There is no comparison of stats for equipment when shopping, crafting, or even when equipping your gear. I found this to be extremely annoying.  I would craft an item, then have to go into the character menu to equip it and see how it would change my stats.  If the item wasn't up to par, I would then just reload the game and re-craft the item which was hopefully better. You also can't preview stats of the item you are crafting which is irritating.  The same works for when you are buying gear at the shop in that there is no comparison between the item you are buying and what's equipped.  Speaking of the shop, there really isn't much that you need to buy other than crafting materials.  All the gear that you craft will be better than what you can buy.  This is common in RPG's, but normally it's towards the end of the game, but here it is right from beginning.  The stat comparison feature must not be available with RPG maker, although I'm not sure why because it was common in this era of games, but the lack of this feature is the worst part of this game.  It is tedious and irritating.

Although the main characters are written beautifully and fully explored, everyone else in the story is kind of bland especially the villains.  The main story itself was nothing original and kind of a bore.  I don't think it was delivered badly, I just didn't find the content exciting or moving.  

Lastly, I felt that the game scaled too high at the end. I played on normal throughout, and didn't grind levels, made some decent/powerful gear here and there, and when I got to the final boss I was completely obliterated.  On my second attempt, I massively upgraded my gear, still not to the point where I have everyone decked out with dragon scale, but had a good array of equipment, and was still getting crushed.  I felt that there was a large gap between the entire game and the final boss.  

Overall this is a fun and well made JRPG.  If you are a fan of the genre it is certainly worth checking out and you will get many hours of enjoyment.

Echoes Of Aetheria is a independent steampunk fantasy R.P.G. adventure game developed by Dancing Dragon Games and published by Degica. You take on the role of Lucian, a soldier in the army of Sandraka who is attending the wedding of his brother to the princess of the neighboring kingdom of Sayunaa. During the ceremony, a vicious assault takes place and in the melee the Sayunaan bride is kidnapped and wisked away through the city to parts unknown. Skilled with a blade and fleet of feet, Lucian immediately gives chase to the kidnappers and attempts to retrieve the bride to be at all costs. This series of unfortunate events sets Lucian on an epic quest across the realm as war breaks out and allegiances are tested whilst a new nation is created. Prepare for an adventure filled with conflict, betrayal, love and redemption in this powerful story-rich RPGMaker title.
 
[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

This game uses the classic R.P.G. formula so your character earns skill points as tasks are completed and battles are fought and won. These skill points can then be applied to upgrade the potency of a number of abilities that your party gains as they venture about. The choice of what abilities to use from a long extensive list is completely up to you and your particular playstyle. The combat is turn-based and initiates when your group and a enemy or enemies come into contact with one another. The battles in this game are strategic and alot of fun while also remaining quite challenging in the process. You definitely rely on your party as a whole to use their unique individual abilities and skills in unison in order to come out victorious especially against the more powerful adversaries that you will face over the course of the story. 

Speaking of story, this is where the game truly makes the most impact in my opinion. Echoes of Aetheria is such a deep narrative driven game that immediately grabs you from the start and maintains a stranglehold on your emotions while this magnificent drama plays out. Humor, romance, conflict, betrayal and loss are just some of the many aspects of this intriguing fantasy adventure. The title also encourages exploration as there are a number of hidden items such as collectibles, crafting materials and other useful things that can only be found if you take some time to wander around and look for them. As far as crafting goes, the crafting system in this title is robust allowing you to create many different types of weapons and armor for your group some of them quite powerful if you have the appropriate materials. All in all, despite being a RPGMaker game, this title provides a good amount of gameplay for the enthusiast R.P.G. fan in my opinion.

[h1]VISUALS[/h1]

As a RPGMaker title I found this game to be quite impressive graphically. The artwork on the main characters during dialogue is superb with very impressive fantasy inspired hand drawn images that noticeably change facial expressions as they speak. Equally of note are the fantastic visuals for the battle sequences of which you will fight many during the course of the game. The sprites feature bright beautiful colors, wonderful animation as well as impressive sound effects. The battlefields are also excellent as are the many varied locations that you visit throughout the kingdom of Aetheria. Bustling cities, vast deserts, lush forested regions, steam punk inspired airships, there are just so many different locations to wander as your journey progresses. The developers used the RPGMaker assets to their full advantage and the production value of this game really shows that effort. In my opinion, this is one of the best if not "THE" best RPGMaker title available on Steam as far as visual presentation is concerned. 

[h1]SOUND[/h1]

Boasting a wonderful orchestral soundtrack Echoes Of Aetheria presents a terrific musical score with tracks appropriate for combat, exploration and emotionally tense moments in the narrative. Also of note are the sound effects that are equally well done which when combined with the music create an excellent aural presentation for the game.
 
[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]

Dancing Dragon Games continues to impress me with yet another wonderful addition to their amazing stable of high quality fantasy games. I absolutely loved "Skyborn" and I think this title actually outshines that amazing game. The intriguing storyline, addictive turn-based combat and highly memorable cast of endearing characters make for a gaming experience that should not be missed for a true fan of the roleplaying game genre. This title is an excellent example that great R.P.G.'s can come from highly talented independent developers with smaller budgets and don't have to be dubbed as a "AAA" title from some globe domineering developer and world-wide game publishing company. I had just as much fun playing this title as I did with other more popular well-known and highly budgeted roleplaying games which I won't mention in this review. With that said, replayability is adequate especially if you want to procure all the achievements. 

The only downside in the gameplay is that you may get lost on some of the maps as you try to backtrack or make sure you explore every area before leaving or moving the story forward which can be frustrating for someone who doesn't want to spend the extra time walking around in circles. As far as options go, there are the aforementioned Steam Achievements to hunt down and Steam Trading Cards to collect. Also, there's a soundtrack filled with a brilliantly composed musical score and the Echoes Of Aetheria strategy guide for people who want to find all the secrets in the game. In conclusion, with a deep story, wonderful R.P.G. mechanics, fantastic visuals and fun combat, Echoes Of Aetheria is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to fantasy, roleplaying and story-rich gamers!

First of all, let me say that I bought this game because I enjoyed Skyborn and saw it was the latest game by the same developer.  Skyborn was quite good, and after seeing some screenshots of the battle system, combined with fact that generally developers get better with experience, I went in expecting this one was gong to be awesome.  

And in a sense it's pretty good, however there's a small handful of things that bother me so much that I just can't really recommend it to people in its current state:

1) Skyborn had some really weird map designs with excessive amounts of nonsensical waterfalls, illogical floating land chunks, bizarre bridge/dock networks hovering above parallaxing backgrounds that felt so out of place they actually broke my immersion in the game world at times.  I was hoping this wouldn't be a thing in this game as well, but already into the first forest, there it is again.

2) This is the big one.  Equipment management is utterly atrocious.  Crafting is a shot in the dark or consult-the-guide experience just like it was in Skyborn, however this game actually took things a step backward and also made shops LESS informative than they were in Skyborn.  There is no (apparent) way to see if a given piece of equipment in a shop is better or worse than what a character is using without going back, manually viewing their equipment in the menu, then returning to the shop to check the new item's stats.  In Skyborn, shops at least showed an up/down comparison of the item's HP against similar items worn by the party, but that's gone in this game.

2.5) Similarly, the items-possessed counter in shops doesn't count equipped items, so if your only Steel Helm is equipped on someone, the "Possessed" counter in the shop will show that you have 0 Steel Helms.  I ended up buying something someone was already using because of this.  Good thing I saved first.

Otherwise, it's a good game.  Some of the better points include:

1) Just like in Skyborn, the story is pretty well-told.

2) The characters and the plot are interesting enuogh that I'd like to know what happens to each of them.

3) The battle system is a straight upgrade over Skyborn's semi-basic front view, as it introduces a nice tactical grid and targeting mechanics that make character and enemy positions important.  Each character feels unique and useful in combat, although the healer (currently) feels a little underwhelming, but maybe that changes later.

Overall, it's game I want to like, but previously-mentioned issue--the lack of transparency in equipment management--is why I just can't give this game a positive review at the moment and am tempted to just walk away from the game without finishing it.  Hopefully it was just an oversight and will change at some point, but until then, maybe try it if it's on sale, otherwise wishlist it, wait, and see.

Echoes of Aetheria von Dancing Dragon Games (Link: http://www.dancingdragongames.com ) ist einer dieser kaufbaren Titel, ein Spiel das sich mit seinem Pixel-Look an Japanische Rollenspiele (kurz JRPG) wie Final Fantasy IV-VI oder Nintendos Fire Emblem anlehnt. Das bedeutet, dass eine Gruppe schillernder Charaktere ein spannendes Abenteuer erlebt und lernt was wahre Loyalität bedeutet und das Krieg meistens doof ist … sagen die Leute, die den größten Teil ihrer Zeit damit verbringen Monster und Bösewichte mit Schwerter und Magie in Grund und Boden zu stampfen. Zumindest reflektieren sie an einer Stelle über die Widersprüchlichkeit ihrer eigenen Weltsicht.

Echoes of Aetherias Geschichte ist gut. Richtig, richtig gut. Natürlich erfinden die Entwickler das Rad nicht neu, im Gegenteil, eigentlich benutzen sie die Formel jedes JRPG seit Final Fantasy IV: böse Nation überzieht Welt mit Krieg,  gute Nation kämpft gegen die Bösen und im Hintergrund gibt es eine dritte Partei, bei der alle Fäden zusammenlaufen. Ist das Schlimm? Natürlich nicht, den Echoes baut seine Handlung um dieses bekannte Gerüst auf und spinnt eine komplexe Geschichte um das Thema Macht und wie nicht nur die Gierigen sie missbrauchen können. Das spiegelt sich auch in den Charakteren wieder, die sich damit arrangieren müssen, dass auch sie Einfluß und militärische Stärke benötigen, um die Welt vor der Zerstörung zu retten. Das gibt ihnen eine gewisse Komplexität, die mich immer zum weiterspielen antrieb. Ich wollte wissen wie es ausging und kann mit Überzeugung sagen, dass die Geschichte von Echoes of Aetheria eine der Wenigen ist, an denen ich nichts auszusetzen habe … und wenn doch, fällt es nichts weiter ins Gewicht. Das ist einfach ein schönes Garn, das auch über sehr gutes Gameplay verfügt.

Das dreht sich meistens um Rundenkämpfe, die ein gewisses Maß an Taktik von mir abverlangen. Anstatt nur die beste Rüstung und das schärfste Schwert zu kaufen, geht es vor allem darum die richtigen Skills einzusetzen, von denen jeder Charakter 33 besitzt. Die richtige Kombination aus Heilzaubern und Attacken führt zum Sieg, aber Vorsicht, selbst der flächendeckende Feuerzauber kann zum Fluch werden. Besonders zum Schluss hin, sollte man einfache Monster nicht unterschätzen. Die Balance stimmt, einzig die Endkämpfe sind wirklich extrem schwer, selbst auf dem mittleren von drei Schwierigkeitsgraden. Ich denke, es ist keine Schande, für den letzten Kampf auf leicht zu schalten, da sich nur der Schaden den die Endgegner einstecken können ändert und sie immer noch gut austeilen.

Die Musik des Spiels lädt zum mitsummen ein. Mein Highlight sind jedoch die Modelle der Gegner in den Kämpfen, die kreativ und beeindruckend aussehen. Der Rest des Spiels wird mit Standard-Modellen des RPG-Makers dargestellt. Wer sich also nicht an einem bunten Pixel-Look stört und Spiele dieser Art gespielt hat, wird auch weiterhin seine Freude daran haben. Mein einziger Kritikpunkt, sind plötzlich auftauchende Rechtschreib- und Grammatikfehler, die mir im letzten Viertel des Spiels auffiellen und mich ein bisschen aus der Handlung reißen. Ich hoffe, dass Dancing Dragon Games die Fehler selbst zwei Jahre später ausmerzt. Echoes of Aetheria hätte es verdient perfekt zu sein. Auf seine Art ist es das schon.

I have a soft spot for RPGMaker games. Good ones evoke a sense of nostalgia for simpler times when playing a JRPG was a rare treat. Echoes of Aetheria falls under the "great" category for me, in large part due to the excellent soundtrack by the creator, and the original art that goes along with it. Echoes does not feel like a cheap cash-in game using nothing but RPGMaker assets; it feels fresh and unlike anything else I've ever played on the platform.

The writing in Echoes is passable, but very conversational. Some of it is anachronistic, but it flows well and characters feel natural. 

Character progression is interesting and forces you to make choices for the purpose of battle. You can't use it all, so you have to develop strategies per character, and try to synergize with the rest of the party. If you can manage to break that system you can wreck everything in your path. If you struggle with it, battles may be a bit more difficult. On the subject of difficulty, there are several options so everyone has a challenging experience.

What really makes Dancing Dragons' games for me is the soundtracks. The original compositions always evoke feelings of adventure or mystery in the perfect way. The battle themes perfectly encapsulate the struggle and the quieter exploration themes don't overpower. 

My only complaints are with the engine itself; issues such as partial controller support, scaling, etc persist that have been solved in newer RPGMaker releases either through scripts or the engine itself (i'm not an expert on this subject so I'm just guessing). 

Every Dancing Dragon Games release has improved on the last, so I can't wait to see what they do going forward.
